Say what you will about America’s police forces, but they are loyal – often to each other, and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle . And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.
A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.
If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because Electrek readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV, which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm, along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles – which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence, and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about – and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score , so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.
A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear – and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue .
A number of photos were originally taken by Dorian Jzak and posted to the Emergency Vehicles Photography Facebook page earlier this week. I included a screencap below, in case it disappears, and clicking here will get you to the original post with more high-res images .
2027 Silverado 9C1 PPV

source_document.body:
Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.
The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.
It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”
My mini-truck from China in its first year, not a scratch on it (yet)
I gave an update after the first year , showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.
So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here . Trust me, you’ll want to.
Five years of actual work
First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.
Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.
Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.
My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.
By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.
Filling the electric truck’s bed with a NESHER L880 electric loader makes for the quietest work site ever
We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.
The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.
But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.
And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).
The truck is more at home on dirt roads or pasture than paved streets
So, what’s actually broken after five years?
Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.
The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.
I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!
Of course, not everything is perfect.
The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.
Florida is a very wet state and the truck has to deal with the rains and the high humidity
The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.
Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video .
The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.
One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.
And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.
There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.
It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.
That hydraulic dump bed is one of the best features. Let’s see your F150 do that…
What about all that Chinese steel rusting away?
One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.
To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.
Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.
The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.
A recent photo showing the yellowing of the tail light lenses from daily UV exposure at the lowest latitudes in the US
The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).
We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.
After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.
Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.
Running my NESHER L1400 electric loader in excavator mode and using the truck to move the digging spoils
Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.
You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.
Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.
Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.
Dump bed strikes again!
The real test: What does my dad think?
Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.
And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.
He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.
In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.
It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV , which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.
But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.
My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.
A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.
Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.
Was it really $2,000, and was it worth it?
Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.
Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).
Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.
And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.
So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.
If you aren’t towing a boat with it, then do you really have a truck?
Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.
Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.
It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.
This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.
But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.
I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.
The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.
I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.
Top comment by RedQuill
Liked by 3 people
So maybe something like $100 a month or less amortized? Sounds like not a bad deal
View all comments
Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.
My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.
When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.
Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

2026 SEMA Show • Nissan Returns to the Annual SEMA Show Featuring a 300-HP Sentra Spec-V Revival Concept, Two Z Cars
1980 Porsche 911 SC Transformed Into a Track-Focused Performance Car Is Ready For a New Owner
10 photos
Photo: Garage Kept Motors / Instagram
Sitting proudly in the inventory of Grand Rapids, Michigan-based Garage Kept Motors , this air-cooled 1980 Porsche 911 SC is now a feisty track machine ready to dominate its opponents.
The Porsche Mission S, the latest concept from the premium German automaker, was shown off cruising the streets of New York City , where it also had its world premiere, and fans are already checking out their bank accounts to see if there’s enough cash for an example. That’s the future of the sports car brand, for sure, but what about the past?
Well, some folks only have eyes for the air-cooled era, and here’s an example to quench that thirst – a 1980 Porsche 911 SC that has been thoroughly modified. The automaker first introduced the new version of the 911, called the 911 SC, back in 1978, with the moniker appearing for the first time since the 356SC – with the moniker allegedly standing for Super Carrera.
This unit retains the unmistakable profile and personality of the classic air-cooled 911 but with a side of performance for the track, and it’s finished in a great-looking shade of baby blue over a matching interior with a single black and carbon fiber Sparco racing bucket seat nestled inside the roll caged interior.
It is motivated by a 3.2L short-stroke flat-six, jumping toward a “significant performance upgrade over the original 911 SC engine,” and it’s paired with a Porsche 915-series five-speed manual transmission, allowing for a “particularly engaging combination on a winding road or circuit.” The exterior and interior are all about track use, with an aggressive aerodynamic treatment, prominent No. 54 competition graphics, and a stripped-out cabin
There’s also an extensive list of modifications, which includes Corolla Rods, Mod S Cam, and Headers, new windows, belts, and a fuel cell, adjustable Koni sport shocks, a new one-inch anti-roll bar at the front and rear, fiberglass doors, Forgeline wheels, PMO carburetors, and 911 Turbo brake calipers, plus Chris Foley of Tangerine Racing Stage 1 mufflers.
Of course, “with its 3.2L short-stroke flat-six, 915 5-speed manual transmission, full roll cage, Sparco racing seat, aggressive aerodynamic package, and competition-inspired appearance, this 1980 Porsche 911 SC is a purpose-built interpretation of the classic air-cooled 911. It offers the look and feel of a vintage Porsche transformed into a serious track-day machine,” according to the dealership.
That also means it won’t sell cheap – which is why we’re not surprised by the $59,900 asking price. So, what do you think? Is it worth the hustle, or should we look for something else that can be used both on and off the streets and tracks of the world, like the Toyota GR Corolla, for example?

Via // Garage Kept Motors

source_document.body:
2026 SEMA Show • 2028 Mitsubishi Outlander Diamond Trail Edition: How Does It Compare to Other Adventure Crossovers?
Canadian Gearhead Bought Survivor 18k-Mile HUMVEE Just To Be Cool at Car Meets, Did He Nail It?
63 photos
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat
What the coolest military vehicle of all time? You can’t chose planes, ships, tanks, drones, submarines, helicopters, motorcycles, horses, hot air balloons, or anything along those lines. In fact, stick to four-wheel vehicles. The Willys Jeep? Mmmm… good one. In fact, great call, but how about something more contemporary? Like, say, its grandson, the HMMWV. Catchy military acronym, right? That’s why soldiers called it, in the most army-style jargon, the Humvee.
When the United States military realized in 1979 that its aging fleet of tactical trucks could no longer keep pace with modern mechanized warfare, the Pentagon drafted specifications for a radical replacement. The High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle, universally known as the Humvee, was conceived to consolidate the roles of the M151 Jeep, the M561 Gama Goat, and various Dodge utility pickups into one single, unstoppable, all-terrain platform.
AM General won the initial prototype contract in 1981 and began mass production at its Mishawaka, Indiana facility on January 2, 1985. Since then, over 281,000 units have rolled off the assembly line, serving in the 1989 invasion of Panama, the Persian Gulf War, Somalia, the Balkans, the War in Afghanistan, the Iraq War (both of them), and the Russo-Ukrainian War, while spawning the civilian Hummer H1 in 1992, followed by the H2, H3, and GMC Hummer EV.
Engineered around a single shared chassis, the military workhorse accommodated 15 distinct configurations, including two-door and four-door troop and cargo carriers, weapons platforms, ambulances, shelter carriers, and TOW missile launchers. Early models relied on a naturally aspirated 6.2-liter Detroit Diesel V8 generating 150 hp (152 PS) and 250 lb-ft (339 Nm) of torque, paired with a 3-speed GM TH400/3L80 automatic transmission and a two-range New Process 218 transfer case.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Starting in 1994, the upgraded A2 variants received a 6.5-liter Detroit Diesel V8 delivering 160 hp (162 PS) and 290 lb-ft (393 Nm) in naturally aspirated guise, or up to 190 hp (193 PS) and 385 lb-ft (522 Nm) when turbocharged, mated to a 4-speed 4L80-E automatic gearbox. Later GEP Optimizer 6500 turbo-diesels pushed output to 205 hp (208 PS) and 440 lb-ft (597 Nm) to handle heavy armor.
While most surviving military units endured grueling front-line combat, one remarkably preserved 1988 AM General M998 Humvee escaped the battlefield to become an unlikely star on the Canadian car show circuit. Kevin Chauhan, the host of the Classic Car ChitChat YouTube channel, caught up with the truck and its proud owner, Darryl, in Ontario to document how an authentic military utility rig became a crowd-pleasing weekend cruiser.
Finished in its original woodland Chemical Agent Resistant Coating applied in June 1999, this 1988 M998 spent its active-duty career stationed at a United States Air Force base in Florida, as evidenced by the stenciled markings on its split flat glass windshield. Because base logistics required only short perimeter trips rather than cross-country convoys, the odometer shows just 18,000 original miles (28,968 kilometers) accumulated over nearly four decades.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat After being decommissioned in June 1999, the truck sat in dry Florida storage before making its way north into Canada, where it was acquired by a professional working in the film industry. Darryl, a lifelong gearhead who started driving in a three-on-the-tree 1972 Ford F-100 and has owned over 25 pickup trucks, bought the Humvee from the movie prop specialist simply to be the coolest kid on the block. He absolutely nailed it.
Stepping up to the massive truck reveals why it steals the spotlight from shiny Corvettes at Oakville car meets. Built on a rigid boxed-steel frame with a 130-inch (3,302-millimeter) wheelbase and an 85-inch (2,159-millimeter) width, the M998 features a heat-treated riveted aluminum body paired with a heavy forward-tilting fiberglass hood. To save weight over its 5,200-pound (2,359-kilogram) curb mass, AM General fitted zippered canvas doors and a soft top.
Every exterior detail was dictated by battlefield survival and rapid deployment. Up front, a heavy-duty steel push guard secured by oversized hitch pins protects the seven-slot grille and upgraded headlights, flanked by hooded blackout marker lamps designed to prevent aerial detection at night. Massive steel lifting shackles bolted directly through the hood and rear bumper allow the entire 7,700-pound (3,493-kilogram) gross-weight vehicle to be airlifted beneath a military transport helicopter.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Currently configured as a nine-passenger troop carrier with wooden slatted side racks and longitudinal bench seats in the bed, the truck carries two spare 37-inch Goodyear Wrangler military tires in the cargo area. Each wheel assembly houses a solid high-grade polyurethane run-flat insert capable of supporting the truck if the tires are punctured by gunfire, with the pair of spares alone weighing more than 500 pounds (227 kilograms).
Unlatching the heavy fiberglass hood requires releasing two side clamps and folding down the front brush guard to expose the cavernous engine bay. Tucked far back behind a triple-stacked cooling radiator array sits the original 6.2-liter (379-cubic-inch) Detroit Diesel V8 engine, fed by a waterproof 24-volt electrical system with an external jump-start receptacle at the rear.
The drivetrain sits high between the frame rails to grant 16 inches (406 millimeters) of ground clearance, courtesy of portal axles that allow the tires to be inflated on the run, while the truck is rolling along.
Photo: YouTube/Classic Car ChitChat Inside the spartan cabin, a massive central tunnel (the size of a front lawn) houses the 3-speed automatic transmission and transfer case right between the seats, leaving room for an M16 rifle mount by the driver's left knee and a rotary ignition switch that requires no key. Despite lacking a rearview mirror, air conditioning, or sound deadening, the independent double-wishbone coil-spring suspension and portal gear hubs deliver a surprisingly composed ride over rough terrain.
The Humvee is one of those iconic war machines that are likely to never lose their cool, precisely due to its rhino stance and absolutely Zero-BS attitude. Yes, it’s got a face only a mother would love, but it was never meant to be a beauty pageant queen. After all, nobody buys a sledgehammer to put it on display in the living room. And this knight may be flashing a shining armor, but it also rocks a swagger no civilian vehicle can ever match. Ever.

Photo: Motorcar Classics
New York-based Motorcar Classics probably thinks it has you well covered for quick grocery sessions on the way to the local racetrack if you're willing to write a rather small check for this 'unicorn' of enthusiast wagons.
The Mercedes-Benz W124 was the executive car for the premium German automaker in production from 1984 to 1997. It was offered in sedan, station wagon, and coupe or cabriolet form, and the company produced no less than 2.7 million of them in a little more than a decade. This iteration is also notable because, starting with the 1993 facelift, the series was officially renamed the first-generation E-Class.
Mercedes-Benz also started having a closer relationship with the Affalterbach-based AMG during the late 1980s, especially after the massive success of the AMG Hammer 6.0 model, a W124 Mercedes packing a swapped M117 engine. The refreshed Mercedes-Benz E-Class thus gained the official E36 AMG models for the estate, coupé, and cabriolet variants.
It had a 3.2-liter M104 engine bored and stroked to a 3604-cc displacement, featuring racing camshafts and a new exhaust system, bringing along about 25% more power than stock. The cars had a stiffer suspension, quicker shifting for the gears, and a 155-mph limited top speed thanks to the gentleman's agreement between Daimler, BMW, and VW, along with the German Ministry of Transport, to keep the Autobahn limit free.
The E36 AMG was also capable of sprinting to 100 kph or 62 mph in just 7.2 seconds in the best configuration, which isn’t bad at all even by today’s standards. Well, if you ever wanted to have one and still please the missus because you can take thee kids to school and practice with all the groceries in the trunk, here’s your chance to own an ‘unicorn.’
Photo: Motorcar Classics “Offered for sale is an exceptional and ultra-rare 1995 Mercedes-Benz E36 AMG Wagon (S124),” says the description from the dealership, produced initially for the Japanese market even though it retains the left-hand configuration, and one of approximately only 170 units with JDM specification. According to them, “this vehicle represents a unique intersection of practical utility and high-performance AMG pedigree.”
It is finished in a classic Black Pearl Metallic (199U) hue, and this S124 continues to have a “commanding presence enhanced by period-correct modifications,” including wide-body E500 front fenders with matching flared rear arches and a comprehensive AMG styling package. There’s also an aggressive stance courtesy of 18-inch staggered two-piece Monoblock wheels, and there’s also a front Brembo big brake kit to make sure that stopping power will never be a problem.
“This E36 AMG has undergone mechanical and cosmetic refreshing by our team at Motorcar Classics to preserve the legendary pre-merger AMG driving experience and ensure it is ready for you to drive or show with pride. This is a rare opportunity to acquire a fully sorted, turn-key example of one of the most desirable Mercedes-Benz wagons ever built. It stands ready for the discerning collector or enthusiast who appreciates the analog, high-performance character of a true AMG classic,” concludes the company.
Photo: Motorcar Classics The monochromatic look is indeed fabulous if you’re into that sort of look, and the only touches of color on the outside are the chrome trim elements on the grill, the emblems, the exhaust tips, and the wheel surrounds plus the yellow-painted front brake calipers. Inside, the mid-1990s atmosphere is pretty obvious thanks to the abundance of wood veneer used as the main trim element and the black leather embracing the seats and the entire cabin – save for the headliner.
The checkered carpets are a bit tacky, indeed, but at last they’re easily replaceable, while the white instrument clusters are a remnant of a bygone age. By the way, the dealership isn’t braking the bank or asking for an arm and a leg from the buyer: the listing is offered at $54,900, and you can even negotiate via the ‘make an offer’ button. All in all, it may not be a very bad idea.
First of all, it’s highly collectible. Secondly, it’s not overly expensive. Sure, it doesn’t have the power of the latest 2027 Mercedes-AMG E 53 Hybrid Wagon, which, as a high-performance plug-in hybrid luxury station wagon, features an electrified AMG-enhanced 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-six and an electric motor plus a 28.6-kWh battery pack rocking a combined output of up to 604 hp in burst mode. But it also doesn’t cost $95,200 sans destination and options. Also, it doesn’t weigh as much – the E 53 has a big battery pack which enables an estimated 41 miles of EV range, but it carries extra heft at all times.
So, what do you think? Would you take home this old-school premium German station wagon from the middle of the 1990s and cruise around like we’re about to witness the launch of Windows 95 and Amazon and eBay, or go for something more modern but also more expensive and heavier, like the E 53 Wagon?

Man Steals Car, Rams Police Vehicle, Jumps Into Water, AirTag Gives Him No Chance
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
If you need more proof that AirTags have become a must-have anti-theft hardware for car owners, here’s a recent case from North Seattle.
A 38-year-old thief stole an SUV, drove away in seconds, and hoped to escape without being caught without even thinking that every move he made was being followed. An AirTag planted in the vehicle he stole revealed his location allowing the police to rapidly track him down.
The incident happened last week when the SUV owner was just unloading stuff from his car. The thief got into the car through the open tailgate when the owner wasn’t around and pressed the start engine button. Because the owner was nearby, the engine started, so he drove away in just a few seconds.
The owner immediately called 911 and told the police officer who arrived at the scene that an AirTag had been planted into the vehicle. It turns out the AirTag was actively broadcasting its location, meaning there’s a good chance that the thief had an iPhone in his pocket.
AirTags are small, pill-shaped devices that use Bluetooth to connect to nearby Apple devices to use their Internet connection specifically to transmit their locations. They do this through the Find My network, and owners can just fire up the Find My app on their iPhones, iPads, or MacBooks to see the location on the map. AirTags don’t come with a power-off button, and the only way to turn off these trackers is to remove the battery.
AirTags use CR2032 batteries, meaning they don’t need to be recharged. They should last up to several months per every battery.
The SUV owner jumped into the patrol car and provided the officer with the location information offered by the AirTag. In just a few minutes, the officer located the car and approached it. The thief was still inside, and after going in reverse and ramming the police car, he managed to jump outside to run away on foot.
He ended up jumping into Lake Washington, trying to swim away. After realizing he was surrounded only by cold water and police officers - apparently , the thief needed 25 minutes to do this - he decided to get out of the water and surrender to the police. He still didn’t give up, as he provided the police with a fake name. The reason was simple: he had several active warrants.
He was taken into custody and is now facing multiple chargers, including stealing the SUV.
AirTags have once again helped recover a stolen car, and despite the damage caused by the thief, it’s pretty clear that such trackers can come in very handy when the worst happens. If you need advice on where to install an AirTag, here are the best 5 places in your cabin .

Porsche and La Marzocco Shake Hands Again for Home Brewing Station – Homage to the Carrera RS 2.7
17 photos
Photo: Porsche Design
Coffee and cakes, pardon me, cars – I'm hungry – just go together, so well, in fact, that Porsche has shaken hands with La Marzocco once again to pump out a limited-edition espresso machine and accompanying paraphernalia that tells the world you’re a true Porsche fan. If you have a Porsche-dedicated man cave, this one is not to be missed.
Building upon the success of the first generation Porsche and La Marzocco espresso machine and gear lineup (2024), the two brands have decided to spit out their latest lineup of unique coffee goodies, all aimed at lovers of perfectly extracted espresso shots to be enjoyed in the present of a Porsche .
Photo: Porsche Design Deniz Keskin, Director of Brand Management and Partnerships at Porsche AG mentions, “ What unites both brands is a passion for outstanding design, precise craftsmanship and the ambition to create something extraordinary .”
As such, the La Marzocco Linea Micra, an expresso machine I've had the pleasure of using in this life – I used to be a barista, too, among others – has been imbued with aesthetics attributed to the “legendary” 911 Carrera RS 2.7.
The five-speed manual transmission-driven powerhouse weighed just 975 kg (2,150 lbs), spat out a whopping 210 bhp (207 hp) coupled with 188 lb-ft of torque with a 2.7-liter displacement, and could reach 0-60 mph in 5.6 seconds (estimated). Did I mention that it was only limited to 500 units worldwide?
For the Linea Micra, we can see that signature blue and white colorway expressed, with the lower section of the Micra, or the base, covered in the coveted Grand-Prix White- Blue variation. Keep in mind that these “ limited-edition ” babies will only be completed in a number of 150 units.
Photo: Porsche Design But other colorways are also available, too, including Grand Prix White - Green and Tangerine – Black version. These will be limited to 911 units each, so you’ll have some time to catch this wave in case you don’t get your hands on a White – Blue.
Aside from coloration, badging and lettering scream Porsche, not to mention that it’s strapped right to the front of the base of each; any guests you’re making coffee for are sure to ask you about why your machine has the name Porsche running across it.
Instead of answering, you can just say, “Keep exploring it.” As they do, they’ll also see “ Carrera RS ” running along the side of the expresso machine, not to mention those pressure gauges to match. Another badge exists, with “ One of 911 ” on it.
A few other touches that scream Porsche include the cup rail with a “ distinctive ducktail ,” the steamer and hot water twist handles with “ RS ” and “ 2.7 ” engraved on them, and another little badge with the rear of an RS 2.7 etched into it. There’s no doubt about it; whoever is enjoying your coffee will clearly be aware of what and who brewed their black liquor.
Photo: Porsche Design But this espresso maker is not alone; Porsche and La Marzocco went to town with a wide range of accessories and even a clothing lineup that runs with the colorways and texts that are signature to the production line.
One of the most important is the Pico coffee grinder, a piece of gear that, just like the Micra, includes the “ Porsche X La Marzocco ” badging, “ Carrera RS ,” and a sleek design that, while it isn’t filled with Porsche cues, compliments the Micra perfectly. The colorways are made to match, however, with the Grand Prix White pairing well with all three machines, and the Orange and Black one with only its counterpart.
All of this is built to the standard that has kept La Marzocco alive since 1927, a clear signal that the gear is worth the cash, and oh what cash. As you read the next paragraph, keep in mind that a standard Micra sells for around €3,000 ($3,360).
At this time, Porsche has these babies up for grabs on their website, with the Pico going for a starting price of $2,125 (€1,900) and the Micra popping of at no less than $7,911 (€7,060), so you’ll be drinking coffee out of a $10K setup, at least. I mean, you have to get the matching cups and all that jazz. Why not go for a RS 2.7 1:18 scale model at $485 and the ESG glass panels with “ Carrera ” at $1,735.
Photo: Porsche Design One thing I do need to point out is that the Grand Prix White – Blue colorway doesn’t seem to be available on the Porsche Design website, so you may need to get in touch with them directly to see if there are even any still up for grabs.
For the limited edition run, Porsche and La Marzocco also reveal a barista towel set, coffee tin, glass coasters, T-shirts, hats, and even notebooks with accompanying pen. Did I mention the socks?
As you’ve figured it out by now, all this is aimed at home use, at best, a little private office, so don’t go thinking that you’re about to open up a Porsche or Carrera-tribute café in your area with the Micra and Pico; you need some serious espresso machines for that. Would you drop this much cash on a home brewing setup?

iPhone Update Makes Google Maps and Waze More Difficult To Use on CarPlay
6 photos
Photo: reddit user 77Squares
iOS 27.2 is now available for download with so many improvements for iPhone owners, but on the other hand, it also looks like it comes with bad news for CarPlay users. This is because a glitch that affects Google Maps and Waze is seemingly part of this update, making the two navigation apps significantly more difficult to use on infotainment screens.
Several discussion threads on reddit ( 1 , 2 ) highlight a bug that causes the journey information panel to cover the vehicle icon in Google Maps and Waze. The right edge of this panel blocks the navigation arrow or a custom vehicle icon from showing up on CarPlay, and this doesn’t appear to be an app-specific issue.
The first reports appeared shortly after the release of iOS 27.2, but several users claim the issue has been around since at least iOS 27 shipped in September. I don’t see this glitch in my car when I use an iPhone running iOS 27.1, but I do see it when I run Google Maps and Waze with a smartphone that has already been updated to iOS 27.2.
Users explain on reddit that this behavior happens regardless of the iPhone model, with the original post revealing that they run CarPlay with an iPhone Duo. I use an iPhone 15 Pro (and I don’t see the bug, though I haven’t updated to iOS 27.2 yet), while my wife, where the bug happens, has an iPhone 16 Pro Max that’s already up-to-date.
Because this isn’t an app-specific glitch, the issue seems to reside in iOS, and because it’s Apple’s walled garden at fault here, there’s not much we can do. If it’s a navigation app template issue, the only way to fix it is with another update that prevents the journey information panel from overlapping the vehicle icon.
Unfortunately, Apple is still tying CarPlay updates to iOS updates, meaning that this issue won’t be fixed unless the company ships another operating system update. This will likely happen in the coming weeks, especially as iOS 27.2 is a major update, and smaller bug-fixing builds typically follow shortly.
For now, no workaround is known to exist, so if you haven’t updated to iOS 27.2 and would rather avoid this bug, the only recommendation is to delay the installation of the new build.
On the good side, Google Maps is getting the fall 2026 update with autumn colors for the trees displayed on the map. This visual update is only live for users who have already received the immersive navigation update, and Google says that only those in metro areas in the United States will see the new colors. This is a limited-time update, and Google Maps will return to the typical tree theme in December.

I Gave Up on YouTube Premium and Now I Love Brave: What CarPlay Users Must Know
8 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
I wouldn’t blame anyone for searching for YouTube Premium alternatives after the latest changes happening in this space. Not only is the Premium tier getting more expensive, but the family subscription has been the subject of changes that caused so much controversy worldwide.
That’s how many people end up trying out Brave. I decided to do the same after Google started enforcing the household rule for YouTube Premium Family accounts - I still don’t think that requiring all family members to live under the same roof makes any sense, considering this rarely happens, so why not rename this tier to YouTube Premium Household? - and Brave was my first stop.
However, because I was using YouTube Premium particularly in my car, where the included YouTube Music subscription came in so handy, Brave had to check several important boxes. It turns out it does this with flying colors, so here’s what every CarPlay user must know if they are pondering giving up on YouTube Premium and YouTube Music for Brave.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution What’s Brave? Before anything else, what is Brave anyway?
Unlike YouTube and YouTube Music, Brave is an application, not a service. It’s a replacement for the YouTube and YouTube Music apps, so you can still connect to the two services, only that you’re using a different app.
Brave is a browser, meaning it was built to let you browse the web. It is primarily a replacement to Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Apple’s Safari on pretty much any platform out there, including desktop and mobile. It comes with dedicated versions for Android and iOS.
But this is where things are getting interesting. The thing that makes Brave such a fantastic tool is its advanced YouTube support. If you launch this browser and point it to youtube.com, you’ll end up getting the same experience as if you were paying for Premium. No ads, no interruptions, nothing. There are lots of settings in Brave specifically aimed at YouTube users, so make sure you check them out should you decide to check it out.
But what does Brave and YouTube have to do with CarPlay?
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution As I said, I needed a fully-featured YouTube Music replacement, and I rapidly discovered that Brave does this very well thanks to the integrated playlist support.
The way this feature was built is fantastic. Brave allows you to create playlists by loading YouTube and going to the song you want to listen to. You just add it to the playlist using this dedicated button in the address bar, and that’s pretty much it.
The next time you launch Brave, you can tap the playlist button, and instead of loading youtube.com again, you can just access the songs you’ve previously added to your playlists. Brave also offers the ability to create multiple playlists and group songs more effectively. For example, I created playlists for road trips, night driving, and for my kid, so I can browse them easily depending on what I want to listen to.
Brave on CarPlay Brave comes with dedicated support for CarPlay, so when you connect your iPhone to your car, you can just fire up the browser. But instead of browsing the web - browsers aren’t yet supported on Apple’s car experience - Brave plays the role of a media app. It lets you access those playlists that you previously created on your iPhone, so you can listen to any song directly from CarPlay.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution As you can see in all these screenshots, Brave uses the media app template on CarPlay, so it looks and feels just like Spotify and YouTube Music. The only difference is that your songs come from YouTube.
The only major shortcoming is that you must create those playlists, so you need to add every song to a playlist before you can enjoy it on CarPlay. If you don’t want to do this, you can just point Brave to a YouTube video, tap play, and then lock your phone to listen to it on CarPlay. Because Brave also allows background audio on YouTube - just like YouTube Premium - you can start listening to a song and lock your phone to manage the playback from CarPlay.
This feature comes in handy especially for long house mixes if you’re into this kind of stuff. Otherwise, if you just want to listen to music, you can just create those playlists.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Here’s a tip if you’re starting to add new songs to your playlists: make sure these songs come from official channels rather than accounts reposting them. The chances of the tunes being removed from YouTube are much lower, so you won’t end up with empty spots in your playlists.
The only feature that I’m missing now is YouTube Music recommending other similar options. I’m still keeping my individual YouTube Premium subscription, but for everything else, Brave is just the perfect replacement that makes so much sense on CarPlay. With a little work, you won’t even feel like you’re missing out on anything in your car.

1966 Chevy Impala Convertible Has the Right Engine, Shipping Will Cost a Fortune
21 photos
Photo: eBay seller class-car.now
1966. That’s the model year that should easily catch the attention of many diehard Chevy fans. Convertible. That’s the body style that certainly appeals to those in the market for an Impala.
This specimen checks both boxes and also adds another one: the right engine under the hood.
The car is searching for a home, assuming someone out there is willing to dig deeper into its past and figure out the information that wasn’t included in the eBay listing. What we know is that the car is already in pretty good shape, and based on the photos shared online by the dealer in charge of finding a buyer, you won’t spend more dollars to turn it into an occasional driver.
Photo: eBay seller class-car.now The first thing I always remember when seeing a 1966 Chevy Impala is… the Caprice. Chevrolet promoted the Caprice to a stand-alone series after previously offering it as an Impala version.
This made sense in so many ways. Chevrolet used the same approach in 1958 when it launched the Impala, and because this first attempt worked like a charm, the GM brand was confident that the Caprice would also become a hit. The Impala was first a Bel Air version, and the Caprice was first an Impala version.
This strategy both lasted for only one year, with the Impala and the Caprice graduating to a stand-alone series only a year later.
Photo: eBay seller class-car.now While the Caprice started gaining traction, the Impala continued to be one of the engines that pushed Chevrolet to 2.2 million cars sold in 1966. This was still a drop from the previous year, but the full-size lineup still accounted for no more, no less than 1.5 million cars.
This Impala probably wears a previous restoration, and I’m not sure how original it continues to be. The dealer says the car is powered by a 396 Turbo-Fire V8 engine with long-tube headers and a three-speed automatic transmission.
The engine lineup in 1966 started with a six rated at 155 horsepower and a base 283 that produced 195 horsepower. The list of optional engines included no more, no less than seven choices. The top configurations were the L35 - a 396 rated at 325 horsepower, the L36 - 427 cubic inches and 390 horsepower - and the L72 - also 427 cubic inches but with 425 horsepower.
The L72 was the most expensive engine in the entire lineup, carrying an extra price tag of $312, so it goes without saying that it didn’t make its way to many Impalas.
Photo: eBay seller class-car.now Otherwise, it’s hard to find a very good reason to walk away from this Impala. It’s a convertible with a black convertible top and black vinyl upholstery, so the red-on-black-on-black setup is one of the main selling points.
The car has 46,000 miles on the clock, but as I said earlier, there are just too many mysterious bits that a potential owner would have to decrypt before even thinking of making an offer.
I think it’s a no-brainer that the car has already been restored, but I also don’t think that buying this Impala without additional data isn’t as straightforward as the dealer probably expects it to be.
The 396 is indeed a major selling point, but there are lots of questions that must be answered in this department, too. Is this the original engine? Do all numbers match? Has the engine ever been rebuilt?
Photo: eBay seller class-car.now A 1966 Impala wasn’t by any means affordable, and some versions continue to sell for high dollars if they check the right boxes. Super Sports are still particularly desirable, especially with the top L72 under the hood, while convertibles are among the most sought-after non-SS Impalas.
Certain options also make these cars more valuable. For example, air conditioning was available for $364 back in the day, while power steering could be had for $95. Power windows cost $100, while power brakes were up for grabs for $42. An AM/FM stereo system cost $239.
This Impala has air conditioning, power steering, power brakes, and possibly other goodies, and this is another part that you should investigate thoroughly. It’s unclear what you’ll find when you open the door of this car, so go ahead and call the dealer to arrange a live inspection if you’re interested in the car.
Photo: eBay seller class-car.now As for the price, I think this Impala is priced correctly, as the dealer is willing to let it go for less than $20,000. The price is firm, so the Make Offer option is not available this time on eBay.
Now, here’s the worst part if you live in the United States and want the car in your garage. This Impala is parked in Bristol, the United Kingdom, so shipping it back to the States will cost quite a lot. The costs of a live inspection are also pretty high, so call the seller to discuss all your options.
